title: Taiwan: The 130 km Strait the World Fears a War Over

minor: 'For decades, both air forces mostly kept to their own side of it' has no entry in the sources list. It is widely reported, but add a source or attribute it.
'A spine of mountains runs down the east' is loose: the Central Mountain Range runs down the middle, shifted east. 'Down the centre and east' is more exact.
'The coast that faces China' for Kaohsiung and Taichung is acceptable, but Kaohsiung is on the south-west coast and not on the strait's narrow stretch.

'Beijing's white paper ... that Resolution 2758 settled it': the paper's argument is mainly about the 'one China principle'. Keep the wording attributed ('its white paper says') so it reads as Beijing's claim.

shots.title: 92% of *Chips*

headline.text: China fires missiles into the seas around Taiwan

shots.title: August *2022*

shots.title: *130* km of Sea

shots.title: *$10 Trillion* War

shots.vo: Your phone, your car and the price of both depend on this island.
So why does the world fear a war over an island smaller than Switzerland?
The answer starts with a treaty signed in 1895.

document.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki, 17 April 1895
document.highlight: The island of Formosa, together with all islands appertaining or belonging to the said island of Formosa.

shots.title: Treaty of *1895*

shots.vo: Taiwan covers about 36,000 square kilometres. 23.4 million people live on it.
A spine of mountains runs down the east, peaking at Yushan, 3,952 metres high.
So most people, ports and factories crowd onto the western plain, facing China.
Across the water, China's Pingtan island sits about 130 kilometres from the coast near Hsinchu.
Japan's westernmost island, Yonaguni, is about 110 kilometres from Taiwan's east coast.
To the south, Y'Ami, in the northern Philippines, lies about 140 kilometres from Taiwan's southern tip.
Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines form a line US strategists have called the first island chain since the 1950s.
Chinese ships heading for the open Pacific pass through gaps in that line. Taiwan sits in the middle of it.
The strait is also one of the world's busiest lanes: nearly half the global container fleet passed through it in 2022.
CSIS estimates $2.45 trillion of goods passed through it that year: over a fifth of global sea trade.

clip.tags: container, terminal, airport, ship, ocean, drone

shots.vo: And then the chips. TSMC, founded in Hsinchu in 1987, runs its leading plants in Hsinchu, Taichung and Tainan.
In 2019, Taiwan held 92 percent of the world's capacity for chips under 10 nanometres. South Korea held the rest.
Those chips run phones, data centres and the AI systems trained in them, far from this island.
But Taiwan imports about 97 percent of its energy.

stat.label: share of Taiwan's energy that is imported, Energy Administration, 2023

shots.vo: Most of its gas arrives by tanker at terminals in Taichung and Kaohsiung, on the coast that faces China.
One more detail. Taipei still governs Kinmen, about 10 kilometres from the Chinese city of Xiamen...
...and the Matsu islands off Fuzhou, both within sight of the mainland.
How did a government in Taipei come to hold islands off China's coast?
It began with a war fought somewhere else.
Austronesian peoples lived on Taiwan for thousands of years. Dutch traders built a fort near today's Tainan in 1624.
The Qing dynasty took the island in 1683 and named it a province in 1885.
Then Japan beat the Qing in a war fought mostly in Korea and Manchuria.
At Shimonoseki, on 17 April 1895, the Qing ceded 'the island of Formosa' to Japan.

document.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki, Article 2, 17 April 1895
document.highlight: The island of Formosa, together with all islands appertaining or belonging to the said island of Formosa.

shots.vo: Line one: Taiwan became Japan's first major colony, and stayed one for 50 years.
In 1943 at Cairo, the US, Britain and the Republic of China declared Formosa should be 'restored to the Republic of China'.

document.title: Cairo Declaration, 1 December 1943
document.highlight: all the territories Japan has stolen from the Chinese, such as Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, shall be restored to the Republic of China.

shots.vo: On the map, Formosa is shaded as promised to the Republic of China.
On 25 October 1945, the Republic of China took over the island's administration.
Then China's civil war swung against the Republic's government.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a crowded harbour in 1949, long lines of soldiers and civilians boarding transport ships seen from a distance, crates and rifles on the quay, low grey sky, no faces in close-up, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing.
In December, Chiang Kai-shek's government moved its seat to Taipei.
About six weeks earlier, at Guningtou on Kinmen, its troops had stopped a landing from the mainland.
In June 1950 the Korean War began. President Truman ordered the US Seventh Fleet into the strait.

headline.text: Truman sends the Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait

shots.vo: His order: prevent any attack on Formosa, and stop Taipei's own air and sea attacks on the mainland.
In the 1951 peace treaty, Japan renounced 'all right, title and claim to Formosa', without saying to whom.

document.title: Treaty of Peace with Japan, Article 2(b), 8 September 1951
document.highlight: Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.

shots.vo: On the map, Formosa's owner is left blank.
That silence is still argued over, by lawyers and governments on every side.
In 1955, by most accounts, a US Air Force general, Benjamin Davis Jr., drew a line down the middle of the strait.
Line two: the median line. For decades, both air forces mostly kept to their own side of it.
In 1958 the People's Liberation Army shelled Kinmen for weeks. The islands held.

headline.text: Mainland guns open fire on Kinmen

shots.vo: Kinmen stayed governed from Taipei, as it still is today.
In 1971, UN Resolution 2758 gave China's seat to the People's Republic and expelled 'the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek'.

document.title: UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 (XXVI), 25 October 1971
document.highlight: to expel forthwith the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek from the place which they unlawfully occupy at the United Nations

shots.vo: On the map, Beijing's flag replaces Taipei's at the UN.
In 1972 the US acknowledged that Chinese on both sides 'maintain there is but one China and that Taiwan is a part of China', and did not challenge it.

quote.text: The United States acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China and that Taiwan is a part of China. The United States Government does not challenge that position.

shots.vo: On the map, the US line on Taiwan is drawn in words, not borders.
On 1 January 1979, Washington recognised Beijing and cut formal ties with Taipei.

headline.text: US switches recognition from Taipei to Beijing

shots.vo: Months later, Congress passed the Taiwan Relations Act: any non-peaceful move on Taiwan would be 'of grave concern' to the United States.

document.title: Taiwan Relations Act, Section 2(b), 10 April 1979
document.highlight: to consider any effort to determine the future of Taiwan by other than peaceful means, including by boycotts or embargoes, a threat to the peace and security of the Western Pacific area and of grave concern to the United States

shots.vo: Line three is drawn in words: no alliance, but a law promising Taiwan 'arms of a defensive character'.
Recognition drained away. By 2024, 12 governments, counting the Holy See, recognised Taipei.
Taiwan itself changed. Martial law ended in 1987, and in 1996 its voters chose a president directly for the first time.
Before that vote, China fired missiles into the sea off Keelung and Kaohsiung. The US sent two aircraft carrier groups.
That was 30 years ago. On the map, the 1996 missile zones fade and today's drill zones are overlaid.
Beijing's case first, in its strongest form.
Its white paper says Taiwan has belonged to China 'since ancient times', that Cairo returned it, and that Resolution 2758 settled it.
Most of the world's governments recognise the People's Republic as China's sole government.
Its Anti-Secession Law of 2005 allows 'non-peaceful means' if peaceful reunification is 'completely exhausted'.

document.title: Anti-Secession Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 8, 14 March 2005
document.highlight: the state shall employ non-peaceful means and other necessary measures to protect China's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

shots.prompt: a documentary photograph of the moment: Its Anti-Secession Law of 2005 allows 'non-peaceful means' if peaceful reunification is 'completely exhausted'.

shots.vo: In 2022, Xi Jinping said Beijing will strive for peaceful reunification, 'but we will never promise to renounce the use of force'.

quote.text: We will continue to strive for peaceful reunification with the greatest sincerity and the utmost effort, but we will never promise to renounce the use of force.
quote.who: Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Communist Party of China
quote.source: Report to the 20th Party Congress, 16 Oct 2022

shots.vo: Now Taipei's case, in its strongest form.
The People's Republic has never governed Taiwan for a single day. The island has run its own government, army and currency since 1949.
Its president since 2024, Lai Ching-te, says the two are 'not subordinate to each other'.

quote.text: The Republic of China and the People's Republic of China are not subordinate to each other.

shots.vo: Polls by National Chengchi University show the share calling themselves only Taiwanese rose from 17.6 percent in 1992 to 64.3 percent in 2024.

chart.title: An identity that grew
chart.source: Election Study Center, National Chengchi University

shots.vo: Taiwan's own politics split. The opposition Kuomintang favours more talks with Beijing.
The governing Democratic Progressive Party stresses Taiwan's separate rule.
Washington keeps both cases at arm's length. It holds to its One China policy, and sells Taiwan arms.
In 2023 the CIA director said Xi had told the military to be 'ready by 2027' to invade, adding that this was not a decision.

quote.text: President Xi has instructed the PLA, the Chinese military leadership, to be ready by 2027 to conduct an invasion.

shots.vo: Japan is close too. Its nearest island is 110 kilometres from Taiwan.
In November 2025, Japan's prime minister told parliament a Taiwan emergency could threaten Japan's survival. Beijing protested sharply.

headline.text: Tokyo links a Taiwan emergency to Japan's own survival; Beijing objects

shots.vo: Meanwhile, the drills grow. In August 2022, after a visit by US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, China declared six exercise zones around Taiwan.
Since then Chinese aircraft cross the median line often. China's foreign ministry has said there is no such line.
Days after Lai took office in May 2024 came drills Beijing named Joint Sword-2024A.
In October 2024, Taiwan's defence ministry counted a record 153 Chinese military aircraft around the island in a single day.

stat.label: Chinese military aircraft around Taiwan in one day, 14-15 Oct 2024, Taiwan MND

shots.vo: In April 2025, a drill called Strait Thunder-2025A practised blockading ports and energy routes, by the Chinese military's own account.

headline.text: 'Strait Thunder' drill rehearses blockade of Taiwan's ports

shots.vo: The budgets are not close. China's official 2025 defence budget is about $249 billion; Taiwan planned about $20 billion.

chart.title: Twelve to one
chart.source: PRC Ministry of Finance, Mar 2025; Taiwan Executive Yuan, Aug 2024

shots.vo: Sources disagree on China's figure: SIPRI estimated $314 billion for 2024, and the Pentagon also puts it above the official number.

document.title: SIPRI Military Expenditure Database fact sheet, April 2025
document.highlight: China's military spending is estimated at $314 billion in 2024.

shots.prompt: a documentary photograph of the moment: Sources disagree on China's figure: SIPRI estimated $314 billion for 2024, and the Pentagon also puts it above the official number.

shots.vo: Each side says it wants peace. Each says it is preparing for the moment deterrence fails. What would that moment look like on the map?
Scenario one: a quarantine. China's coast guard, not its navy, inspects ships bound for Taiwan's ports, a case CSIS has studied.
Kaohsiung, Taichung, Keelung: the ports a quarantine would test.
Taiwan's stocks of liquefied gas have been reported at about 11 days of use.

stat.label: Taiwan's reported LNG stocks, Ministry of Economic Affairs via Reuters, 2024

shots.vo: The 1979 US law names 'boycotts or embargoes' as of grave concern.
Bloomberg Economics estimates a blockade alone would cut world output by about 5 percent.

clip.tags: container terminal, harbor, container, cargo, port, export, shipping, terminal, industry, logistics, ship, transport, harbour, warehouse

shots.vo: Scenario two: an invasion. Troops would cross at least 130 kilometres of open water.
Analyst Ian Easton counted 14 beaches on Taiwan's coast suitable for a large landing.
By his reading, wind and waves leave two main windows a year: April and October.
A 2023 CSIS wargame ran an invasion 24 times. In most runs it failed, at high cost to every side.

document.title: CSIS, 'The First Battle of the Next War: Wargaming a Chinese Invasion of Taiwan', 9 January 2023
document.highlight: In most scenarios, the United States/Taiwan/Japan defeated a conventional amphibious invasion and maintained an autonomous Taiwan. However, this defense came at high cost.

shots.prompt: a documentary photograph of the moment: A 2023 CSIS wargame ran an invasion 24 times. In most runs it failed, at high cost to every side.

shots.vo: On the map, the stake is the first island chain: held, or with a new gap in its middle.
That is the war Bloomberg prices at about $10 trillion, roughly a tenth of world output.

stat.label: Bloomberg Economics estimate for a war over Taiwan, Jan 2024

shots.vo: Scenario three: the line holds, and the chips spread out.
TSMC opened a plant in Kumamoto, Japan, in February 2024...
...and began volume production in Arizona in late 2024.
Some argue spreading the chips out lowers the stakes for the world.
Others say Taiwan's chips are its best protection, and want them kept there.
In this future, the median line stays, crossed often, and both sides keep arming.
All three roads run through the same 130 kilometres of water.
Both sides preparing for a fight over Taiwan say they do it so the fight never comes.
The map shows how little room 130 kilometres leaves for anyone to be wrong.
Next: the Strait of Malacca, where much of China's imported oil passes.
